hints: Focus on how many lone pairs are on the central atom in each molecule, as lone pairs squeeze bond angles.
Notice that $\text{BF}_3$ has no lone pairs and is trigonal planar, so its angle is the full $120^{\circ}$, clearly the largest.
Compare the two pyramidal or bent molecules left, the one with two lone pairs is squeezed more than the one with one lone pair, giving you smallest to middle.
walkthrough:
**Find the shape of each molecule**

Start by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom. This tells you the electron geometry.

$\text{BF}_3$: 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs = trigonal planar

$\text{NH}_3$: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair = trigonal pyramidal

$\text{H}_2\text{O}$: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs = bent

**Apply the repulsion rule**

Remember the strength of repulsion follows this order:
$$\text{lone pair-lone pair} > \text{lone pair-bonding pair} > \text{bonding pair-bonding pair}$$
More lone pairs means more squeezing, so the bond angle gets smaller.

**Order from smallest to largest**

$\text{BF}_3$ has no squeezing, so it stays at $120^{\circ}$, the largest. $\text{NH}_3$ has one lone pair, so it is squeezed to about $107^{\circ}$. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has two lone pairs, so it is squeezed most to about $104.5^{\circ}$.

Order is: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ < $\text{NH}_3$ < $\text{BF}_3$.

options.A: Correct. H2O (approx 104.5 degrees) is smallest due to 2 lone pairs, NH3 (approx 107 degrees) is middle due to 1 lone pair, and BF3 (120 degrees) is largest with no lone pairs.
options.B: Reversed order. This suggests BF3 is smallest and H2O is largest, which ignores lone pair repulsion. BF3 with zero lone pairs cannot have the smallest angle.
options.C: Swaps H2O and NH3. A common trap is thinking NH3 is more squeezed, but H2O has two lone pairs while NH3 has only one, so H2O must have the smaller angle.
options.D: Puts BF3 in the middle and NH3 as largest. This is wrong because trigonal planar BF3 at 120 degrees is always larger than pyramidal NH3 at about 107 degrees.
